source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving (theory)
finding: Representational Change Theory (RCT). Impasse arises when prior knowledge sets constraints and tight chunks in the problem representation. Persistent failure triggers two repair operations: constraint relaxation (the wider the constraint's scope, the harder) and chunk decomposition (the tighter the chunk, the harder).
numbers: Four experiments on matchstick arithmetic (move one stick to fix a Roman-numeral equation). Problem types A to D, 5-minute limit per problem.
quote: one of the mind's responses to persistent failure
limits: Narrow domain with strong arithmetic priors. The quote is how Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) cite p.1535.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete mechanism for our impasse state: after repeated failure, drop an assumed constraint or split a unit we treated as atomic, instead of searching harder in the same frame.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving (Exp 1A)
finding: Difficulty followed the scope of the constraint to be relaxed: type A easiest, B harder, C hardest. Type D (tight chunk, e.g. split a plus sign) was harder than type A (loose chunk).
numbers: Exp 1A: N=20 German students, two blocks. Problem type main effect F(3,57)=7.11, p<.001; order C<B<A and A<D (B<A p<.05, C<B p<.01, D<A p<.05). Block effect F(1,19)=14.41, p<.01 (more solved in block 2).
limits: Small N. A vs D solution frequency was not significant in some analyses (p=.13 in the summary table); the solution-time difference was highly significant.
agent_relevance: Reframing difficulty is graded. Moves that change a narrow assumption (a value) come first; moves that break a wide assumption (the equation form itself) come last. A restructuring operator list should be ordered by scope.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving (Exp 1B and Exp 2 replications)
finding: The predicted order C<B<A and A<D held in a second sample (1B) and in an American sample (Exp 2). Some pairwise contrasts hit ceiling and were not significant.
numbers: Exp 1B: N=38 paid participants (17 male, 21 female); B vs A not significant (96% of A and 90% of B solved; ceiling) but solution time differed. Exp 2 (American students) also gave the predicted order; B vs A p=.14.
limits: Authors' own replications, same lab, same paradigm. Ceiling effects on easy types.
agent_relevance: The ordering is robust within the paradigm, so a scope-ordered relaxation schedule has at least one stable human benchmark.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving (transfer across blocks)
finding: A second encounter with the same problem type removed the difficulty gap. Harder types gained more from the first encounter. The authors read this as constraint relaxation and decomposition carrying over, not as surface similarity.
numbers: Interaction between initial difficulty and transfer found in all four experiments. In Exp 2 the similarity manipulation (same numerals, same order, different) had no measurable effect on transfer: F(3,74)=0.34 for similarity.
limits: Transfer tested within one domain and one session.
agent_relevance: Once a constraint has been relaxed on one problem, the relaxation is reusable on the next. A scaffold could store the relaxed assumption as a note across items, not just the answer.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider & Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving (Exp 3, tautology manipulation)
finding: Showing the equation form that removes the constraint (a tautology such as IV=IV=IV) made type C easy but did not help type D. This separates the two sources of difficulty: relaxing a constraint and decomposing a tight chunk are different mechanisms.
numbers: Regular-first group, block 1: Type C 61% solved. Tautology-first group: all type C solved in block 1. Type D block 1: 61% regular-first vs 69% tautology-first (chi2(1,N=34)=0.22, p=.64); block 2: 92% vs 94%. Type A: 94% vs 97%. Median solve time (s), regular-first: A 32, C 175, D 193; tautology-first: A 37, C 11, D 46.
limits: Exp 3 N=34. Ceiling in later blocks.
agent_relevance: One generic 'think differently' prompt is the wrong tool. A hint that exposes a hidden constraint helps only for constraint-type blockages, not for structural chunk blockages.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42) (Exp 1)
finding: Chunk tightness mattered as RCT predicts, but equation values also mattered, which RCT does not predict. Large value gaps pushed people toward the operator and wiped out most of the chunk effect.
numbers: N=121 (38 male, 83 female). Solved: low-value loose 77% (23/30), low-value tight 43% (13/30; the paper's table shows 11/29, 40%), high-value loose 90% (28/31), high-value tight 77% (24/31). Chunking Wald=8.12 p=.004; Value Wald=8.65 p=.003; interaction ns. First move on a loose-chunk match: 93% low-value loose, 76% low-value tight, 63% high-value loose, 52% high-value tight.
limits: One problem per cell, between-subjects. Text and table disagree on one cell (13/30 vs 11/29).
agent_relevance: Apparent progress cues steer which restructuring is tried. If our agent ranks candidate reframings by a progress score, that score will sometimes surface the right one and sometimes bury it.

source: Ormerod & MacGregor (2020) The complementary roles of knowledge and strategy in insight problem-solving (CogSci 42) (Exp 2, tautology problems)
finding: Standard tautology problems were hard (12% solved) only when the value gap gave no cue. With a high-value gap they reached 62%, close to the reverse-tautology problems. Progress monitoring can substitute for knowledge relaxation.
numbers: N=133 (47 male, 86 female). Standard tautology: low-value 12% (4/32), high-value 62% (21/34). Reverse tautology: low-value 72% (23/32), high-value 77% (28/35). Logistic model chi2(3,N=133)=39.30 p<.001; Tautology Wald=19.33; Value Wald=11.12 p=.001; interaction Wald=5.26 p=.022.
quote: the mind's 'response to persistent failure' is not to try to forget what it knows; it is to try to find something better.
limits: Authors back the progress-monitoring account, so the interpretation is theirs. One problem per cell.
agent_relevance: Competing account: insight needs no special relaxation. After criterion failure, widen the move space and score moves by apparent progress. This is cheaper to implement as code than a relaxation operator.

source: MacGregor, Ormerod & Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: a process model of performance on the nine-dot and related problems (JEP:LMC 27, 176-201), data as reported in Ormerod et al. (2006)
finding: Progress monitoring theory (later called CSPT, criterion for satisfactory progress). Solvers pick moves that maximise apparent progress toward the goal (hill-climbing). Insight problems are hard because the progress-maximising moves lie off the solution path. When no move meets a progress criterion (criterion failure), the solver widens the search space.
numbers: Nine-dot with a given first line: a diagonal first line inside the array gave more solutions than a horizontal line that goes outside: 47% vs 28% (Expt 4) and 65% vs 43% (Expt 5, N=103).
limits: Opened only through the 2006 and 2020 secondary reports, not the 2001 paper itself.
agent_relevance: A codeable impasse detector: count attempts whose progress score stops improving, then switch to a wider move generator. This fits our rule that doubt starts only on a signal.

source: Ormerod, Fioratou, Chronicle & MacGregor (2006) The Remnants of Insight (CogSci 28) (nine-dot replication)
finding: Seeing a solution does not guarantee solving again. Many people recall 'go outside the square' but cannot execute it, and swing between applying that knowledge and hill-climbing inside the array. Forgetting alone does not explain it.
numbers: Earlier: Weisberg & Alba (1981): 5 of 12 failed the nine-dot five months after seeing the solution, 8 of 23 failed after one week. Here (data from MacGregor et al. 2001 Expts 4-5): 10 solved on attempt 1, 7 on attempt 2, 16 failed to solve in two attempts, 11 failed in all 10. Of the 16 early failures: 2 'within', 5 'going outside', 8 mixed.
limits: General public and undergraduates; 30 s per attempt, so not comparable to long-time-limit studies.
agent_relevance: Knowing the reframe is not enough. The agent must be able to execute it. Store the reframe as an executable procedure or worked example, not just as a statement.

source: Ormerod, Fioratou, Chronicle & MacGregor (2006) The Remnants of Insight (CogSci 28) (cheap necklace and six-coin experiments)
finding: A conceptual hint ('destroy in order to create') and a changed spatial layout both failed to give transfer. Easy-to-recode insights (eight-coin: stack in 3D; matchstick: three-part equation) can be re-solved after months. Insights that need several linked concepts cannot.
numbers: Cheap necklace: N=50. Problem variant solved by 5 in the hint group and 6 in the control group. Many participants restated the hint correctly but could not apply it. Six-coin spatial variants: mean solution rates under 20%. Eight-coin re-solved after months (Ormerod et al. 2002, as cited).
limits: Small cell counts. Some counts are garbled in the text extraction (standard-problem solve counts).
agent_relevance: Supports storing solved-problem insights as one executable principle. Hints that state a principle help little when it must be mapped onto a new layout.

source: Wikipedia: Insight (problem solving section)
finding: Gestalt origin: insight as restructuring, linking to another problem-solution pair, releasing blocking past experience, or seeing a larger context. Duncker & Lees (1945) candle problem shows functional fixedness. Hadamard four stages (preparation, incubation, illumination, verification) refine Wallas.
numbers: Metcalfe & Wiebe (1987): warmth ratings predicted progress on non-insight problems but not on insight problems. Segal (2004): a 4-minute break helped as much as a 12-minute break. Wagner et al. (2004): 8 hours of sleep gave twice the insight performance of staying awake. Ovington et al. (2015): almost 20% of respondents reported never having an insight.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, not primary data. Numbers are as the article reports them.
agent_relevance: Insight is a sudden jump that people cannot predict with warmth feelings. The agent should not trust its own 'getting close' signal on insight-type tasks; use external checks.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135, 94-120) (overall effect)
finding: A small positive incubation effect exists on average. Breaks help, but not by much and not for every problem type.
numbers: 117 studies. Weighted mean unbiased effect size 0.29 (SE 0.04; 95% CI as printed 0.21 to 0.39); between-study variance .0834. Funnel plot judged to show no publication bias, so no correction applied. 88 of 117 effects computed directly from means.
limits: Mixed task types pooled. Many included studies were small. Funnel-plot symmetry is weak evidence against bias.
agent_relevance: Temporal breaks are worth little in expectation (d about 0.3). An LLM has no clock-based incubation, so any analogue must come from changing context or representation, not from waiting.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135, 94-120) (moderators: load and problem type)
finding: A low-load interpolated task beat both a high-load task and rest, but only for linguistic problems. Divergent-thinking (creative) tasks showed the largest incubation gain. Visual problems showed smaller gains.
numbers: Studies by type: linguistic 65, visual 35, creative 14. Subgroup mean effect: linguistic 0.22, visual 0.26, creative 0.29 (as read from Table 4). By incubation task: high load 0.24, low load 0.52, rest 0.46. In linguistic studies low load vs rest beta=.54, p<.05. Misleading cues present (n=29) 0.35 vs absent (n=85) 0.32; relevant cues present (n=32) 0.24 vs absent (n=82) 0.34.
limits: Subgroup means read from a table with imperfect text extraction; check before quoting. Moderators are confounded across studies.
agent_relevance: Cheap, undemanding distractors work best. For an agent this argues for a light context switch (a different framing task) rather than a heavy parallel task.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review (Psych Bull 135, 94-120) (preparation length)
finding: Longer preparation (more time on the problem before the break) predicted larger incubation effects, for visual and creative problems but not for linguistic ones.
numbers: Preparation length beta=.03, p<.05. Correlation with effect size: visual r(35)=.40, p=.02; creative r(14)=.60, p=.03; linguistic r(65)=.04, p=.75.
limits: Correlational, across studies.
agent_relevance: An impasse must be real before a break or reset pays off. Reset only after a genuine stall, which matches our doubt-on-signal rule.

source: Gilhooly (2016) Incubation and intuition in creative problem solving (Front Psychol 7:1076)
finding: Reviews theories of incubation: unconscious work (favoured), intermittent conscious work, beneficial forgetting, fresh look. The author favours unconscious work for small knowledge-rich problems. Several results run against the alternatives.
numbers: Sio & Ormerod 117 studies, d=0.29. Strick et al. (2011) 92 decision studies, g=0.224 for immediate incubation. Gilhooly et al. (2012): 8 correlations between interpolated and target tasks, mean r=0.11 (6 positive, 2 negative). Segal (2004): 4 vs 12 minute breaks.
limits: Narrative review by a proponent. Knowledge-lean insight problems and large real-world problems are not covered. Hélie & Sun's model cannot explain breakthroughs without an explicit return to the task.
agent_relevance: Evidence for incubation is mostly about small problems with stored knowledge. It gives no support for long idle time as a general scaffold step.

source: Helie, Sun & Xiong (c.2008) Mixed Effects of Distractor Tasks on Incubation (CLARION, CogSci) (literature review and model)
finding: CLARION has an explicit top level and an implicit bottom level, with bottom-up and top-down learning. Incubation is mainly bottom-level processing. A distractor hurts incubation only if it uses the same modules as the main task. Incubation is not one process, so mixed results are expected.
numbers: Dodds, Ward & Smith (2003) review as cited: 29 of 39 experiments found a significant incubation effect. Olton & Johnson (1976) used seven distractor activities on insight problems and found no incubation effect at all.
limits: This is the distractor-task paper, not the full Psychological Review 2010 model paper. Year is approximate (not printed on the text read).
agent_relevance: Two interacting systems (explicit rule search and implicit association) are a design pattern: run a loose associative pass alongside the strict explicit pass, then integrate.

source: Helie, Sun & Xiong (c.2008) Mixed Effects of Distractor Tasks on Incubation (CLARION, CogSci) (human free-recall test)
finding: Reminiscence (new items recalled after a gap) depended on the distractor. Doing nothing gave the most. Syllogisms and a dynamic control task suppressed it below the no-incubation level.
numbers: Free recall of 50 line drawings, 10-minute gap. F(5,108)=10.65, p<.001. Mean reminiscence: do nothing 7.26; no incubation 4.9; remote association 4.84; perceptual-motor 4.84; syllogistic reasoning 2.47; dynamic control 2.26.
limits: Free recall, not problem solving. Authors propose testing problem solving later.
agent_relevance: Heavy explicit reasoning between attempts can erase the gain from a pause. Do not fill the gap with reasoning chains.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model (Psych Rev 117, 994-1024), as reported in search summaries
finding: Explicit-Implicit Interaction (EII) theory. Explicit rule search and implicit associative processing run together and reinforce each other. The CLARION implementation simulates human data on incubation and insight.
numbers: Not read; no numbers verified.
limits: Seen only through a press summary and citation lists. Full text not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Formal model of the Wallas stages that could be mapped to our states: a strict path plus an associative path with a mixing weight.

source: Wareham (2012) What can (and can't) make problem solving by insight possible? A complexity-theoretic investigation (ICCM poster)
finding: Formalises RCT as search alternating with restructuring operators and proves the problem intractable in general. Only small restrictions on restructuring steps, constraints, active chunks and search steps make it tractable.
numbers: Theorem 1: the restructuring problem (PSRI) is NP-hard even when the allowed number of constraint relaxations is 0 or the allowed number of de-chunkings is 0. Theorem 3: fixed-parameter tractable for the combined parameter set of de-chunk count, search-step count, number of constraints, number of active chunks and chunk-type set size.
limits: A poster; worst-case theory, not human data. Parameter definitions paraphrased from the poster.
agent_relevance: Unbounded 'try every reframing' is hopeless. Cap restructuring depth, number of simultaneous frames and search steps, as in our budget rules.

source: NazoNazo Benchmark: a cost-effective and extensible test of insight-based reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2509.14704) (accuracy)
finding: Japanese children's riddles that need a reinterpretation of wording. 38 LLMs from 2023-2025 stay far below humans, zero-shot, no retrieval. Reasoning models beat non-reasoning ones. GPT-5 is the one model near the human range.
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human-comparison subset; humans n=126, mean 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2). On the subset: non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. On all 201 items: reasoning 19.25% vs non-reasoning 9.42%, odds ratio 2.29 (95% CI 1.99-2.64, p<.0001). Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date correlated positively.
limits: GPT-5 inside the human CI is descriptive only, not an equivalence test. Riddles may be in training data. Versions differ (v1 used 120 riddles).
agent_relevance: Insight-type tasks remain a weak spot for the plain model; a measured gap exists to test the scaffold on.

source: NazoNazo Benchmark: a cost-effective and extensible test of insight-based reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2509.14704) (verification failure)
finding: Models often write the correct answer in their reasoning and then answer differently. The authors call this verification failure, a last-mile failure of endorsement and stopping, not of generation. They also see 'false insight', a confident wrong reinterpretation.
numbers: Verification failures as share of wrong answers: Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 5.23% (9 items), Claude Opus 4 25.00% (35), DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57% (48), Grok 4 39.34% (48). Counted when a gold-answer variant appears literally in the thought log before the final answer.
limits: Literal string matching on thought logs; logs are not guaranteed faithful. Only four models had usable logs. Automated accuracy in this table differs from the main scoring.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a code-side check that scans earlier candidates and requires a held-out test before discarding one. Without a verifier the agent can lose a correct reframe it already produced.

source: NazoNazo Benchmark: a cost-effective and extensible test of insight-based reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2509.14704) (language of thought)
finding: Reasoning in Japanese did not reliably help. The language effect differed by model.
numbers: Grok 4: Japanese thought logs 29.5% correct (33/112) vs English 48.8% (40/82), p=.0071. Claude Opus 4: Japanese 36.7% (16/44) vs English 28.7% (45/157), p=.356. Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview: Japanese 0% (0/12) vs English 11.7% (22/188), p=.369. DeepSeek-R1-0528: 23.1% (46/199) with Japanese logs in all 199.
limits: Language was the model's own choice, so it is self-selected and confounded with item difficulty.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a particular working language helps insight-type tasks; this is model-specific and untested for our agent.

source: Creative problem solving in large language and vision models: what would it take? (arXiv 2405.01453, EMNLP 2024 Findings) (position and object-replacement test)
finding: Position paper linking computational creativity (transformational creativity, OROC task re-representation) to vision-language models. A small test asks the model to choose a replacement object for a missing tool. Models do well when the tool is present and poorly when a creative substitute is needed.
numbers: Nominal group (tool present) accuracy: CLIP-B-32 100%, CLIP-B-16 92%, CLIP-L-14 98%, CLIP-H-14-laion 98%, ViLT-B-32 68%, LLaVA 98%. Replacement group: random choice about 30%; models 'perform poorly' with the plain prompt (values only in a figure). Adding object affordance information helped on average; adding task information was mostly detrimental; task plus affordance gave no big gain. Five core objects (scoop-bowl, hammer-saucepan, spatula-knife, toothpick-safety pin, pliers-scissors), ten random object sets.
limits: Tiny test set, no exact replacement-group numbers in text, models are CLIP, ViLT and LLaVA, not frontier LLMs. Authors call the experiments preliminary.
agent_relevance: Re-describing the object by its affordances is a representation change that helped; stating the task did not. Supports a reframing operator that restates an object or sub-problem by function.

source: Wikipedia: Insight (incubation and individual-difference claims)
finding: Incubation, mood, sleep, mindfulness and EEG findings are listed as support for a distinct insight process. Smith et al. (2009/2010): a 15-minute break helped individuals on rebus puzzles with unhelpful clues. Kounios & Beeman: high gamma-band activity about 300 ms before insight solutions.
numbers: Ren et al. (2011): a 20-minute mindfulness session helped. Lin et al. (2011): men better on insight, women better on non-insight problems.
limits: Wikipedia summary; several effects (sex difference, mindfulness) are single-lab results not checked here.
agent_relevance: Mostly human-physiology findings with no direct agent analogue. The useful part is that insight problems respond to breaks differently from analytic ones.

source: Duncker (1945) On problem solving; Duncker & Lees (1945) Psychological Monographs 58(5); candle problem
finding: Functional fixedness: people see an object only by its usual function, so the box holding the tacks is not seen as a candle shelf. Duncker proposed that solving needs restructuring of the problem representation.
numbers: Not verified here; no percentages from the original read.
limits: Seen only via Wikipedia. Follow-up candle studies not opened.
agent_relevance: Origin of the 'object blocked by familiar role' pattern; a template for function-reassignment reframes.

source: Weisberg & Alba (1981) An examination of the alleged role of fixation in the solution of several insight problems; as reported in Ormerod et al. (2006)
finding: Challenge to the Gestalt special-process view of the nine-dot problem. Telling people to go outside the square did not solve it for most. The authors argue prior-knowledge constraints, not special restructuring, explain the difficulty.
numbers: As quoted in Ormerod et al. 2006: 5 of 12 failed five months after seeing the solution (Expt 1b); 8 of 23 failed after one week (Expt 1c). In 1c, 10 of 23 solved on the first attempt; of the other 13, 6 went outside and 5 of these solved.
limits: Original not opened; figures come from a secondary report.
agent_relevance: A stated insight is not a solved problem. Keep an execution check after the reframe.

source: Kaplan & Simon (1990) In search of insight (Cognitive Psychology), as described in Ormerod & MacGregor (2020)
finding: Insight as search at the level of problem representation. Solvers detect invariants, features that do or do not vary, and use them as cues for moves. Ormerod & MacGregor say it covers idea generation only, not the source of difficulty.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Described second-hand; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Early computational model of insight as heuristic search over representations. Supports treating reframing as another search step with its own cues.

source: Danek & Wiley (2017) and Wiley & Danek (2024), as cited in NazoNazo
finding: Human false insights: a sudden wrong 'aha' held with confidence. NazoNazo uses this to describe LLMs that adopt a wrong reinterpretation with apparent confidence.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Cited via the NazoNazo paper only; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Confidence at the moment of reframing is a weak signal. Require an external test before accepting a sudden reframe.

source: Dodds, Ward & Smith (2003) A review of experimental literature on incubation in creative problem solving, as cited in Helie & Sun
finding: Incubation helped in most but not all published experiments. Longer incubation, preparation and useful clues raised the effect. Misleading clues inhibited it. Distractor effects were unstable.
numbers: 29 of 39 experiments found a significant incubation effect (as cited).
limits: Second-hand citation. Publication bias in the pool is possible.
agent_relevance: Base rate for a pause or reset helping: about three in four published studies, with a small average effect.
